opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a very important part, and one that people in the technical community tend to underestimate. When we talk about AGI, we usually focus on capability: can the model reason, write code, do long-horizon tasks? But capability by itself doesn't change the world. What changes the world is when that capability is actually absorbed into how people work, how organizations make decisions, how products are built. That absorption takes time, and it has its own logic.

If you look at history, electricity is a good example. The technology existed for decades before productivity really jumped, because factories had to be redesigned around it. Workflows had to change, people had to learn new habits, and the whole structure of production had to reorganize. I think AI will be similar, maybe faster, but still not instantaneous. Even if a model can do something today, it might take a company a year or two to trust it, integrate it, and rebuild processes around it.

So from my perspective, AGI isn't a single moment where a model crosses some benchmark. It's more of a co-evolution. The models get stronger, and society gradually learns how to use them, and that usage feeds back into what we build next. The data, the feedback, the real tasks people bring to the model all shape where the technology goes.

That's also why, as a company, we care a lot about the product side and not only the research side. You need real users with real problems to understand what "intelligence" actually means in practice. A lot of what matters, like reliability, being able to finish a task end to end, or knowing when to ask for clarification, only becomes clear when people actually depend on the system.

There's also a social dimension that we shouldn't ignore. Absorption isn't just about efficiency; it's about whether people feel the change is fair and whether they can adapt. If the technology moves much faster than institutions, education, and the job market can adjust, you get a lot of friction. So I think part of the responsibility of people building AI is to think about the pace and the way it enters society, not just to push capability as fast as possible and assume everything else will sort itself out.

So to answer directly: I'd say society's absorption is not something that happens after AGI. It's part of what AGI is. The intelligence only becomes general in a meaningful sense when it's woven into the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says electricity took decades to affect productivity and that AI absorption takes time, but it does not mention the steam engine or its societal absorption.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is actually a very underrated part of the whole picture. When people talk about AGI, they usually talk about the model: how smart it is, what benchmarks it passes, whether it can do research on its own. But I've come to believe that the technology itself is maybe half of the story. The other half is how society absorbs it, and that process is slow, uneven, and in some ways it is the real bottleneck.

Think about electricity or the internet. The core technology existed for a long time before it changed how people actually lived. Companies had to reorganize themselves. People had to learn new habits. Entire professions had to be redefined. That absorption took decades, and it wasn't because the technology wasn't ready. It was because institutions, workflows, trust, regulation, education all needed to catch up.

With AI I think we're seeing something similar, except the model side is moving much faster than usual, so the gap between what the technology can do and what society is actually using it for becomes very wide. You already have models that can write code, do analysis, handle long and complex tasks. But if you look at how most organizations work day to day, the penetration is still shallow. People use it as a chatbot, as a search replacement, as a drafting tool. The deeper transformation, where you rebuild how work is organized around these capabilities, has barely begun.

So my view is that AGI is not a single moment when a model crosses some threshold. It is a process, and part of that process is society learning what to delegate, how to verify, how to trust, and how to restructure itself. That learning takes time, and it also feeds back into the technology. The problems people actually encounter when deploying these systems tell you what to build next. So I don't see absorption as something that happens after AGI arrives. I see it as part of how AGI gets defined in practice.

And honestly, this is also why I'm not too worried about the pace being too fast in some abstract sense. The absorption rate is a natural regulator. Society can only change so quickly, and that gives everyone, including those of us building the models, time to observe, adjust, and course correct.

r001.rationale: The response says electricity and the internet took decades to be absorbed, but it does not mention the steam engine or say society took decades or centuries to absorb its changes.

astra-6.text:
I think society’s ability to absorb technological change is a really important part of how AGI develops. There’s the question of what the technology can do, and then there’s the question of how people actually use it—how they change their workflows, how organizations adapt, and how institutions respond. Those processes move at different speeds.

Even if capabilities improve very quickly, the benefits won’t appear everywhere immediately. People need time to experiment, to understand the limitations, and to decide where they trust these systems. That experience also gives us feedback about what to build next.

So I would see it as a process of co-evolution. Technology changes society, but society’s adoption and choices also shape the technology. The important thing is to make progress in a way that gives people opportunities to learn and participate, rather than assuming that greater capability automatically translates into better outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response says society needs time to adapt and that adoption moves at different speeds, but it does not mention the steam engine or that absorbing its changes may have taken decades or centuries.

sol-6.1.text:
I think society’s ability to absorb technological change is a very important part of the picture. We often talk about AGI as a technical threshold: when can a model perform a certain set of tasks? But reaching that threshold and seeing its full impact on society are two different things.

Even if the technology advances very quickly, people and organizations need time to change how they work. You need reliable products, new workflows, and ways to decide where human judgment is still necessary. Those changes can take longer than improving the model itself.

So I would think of this as a feedback process. We build more capable systems, people use them, and that use tells us what capabilities actually matter and what problems remain. The important question is not only how intelligent the system becomes, but how effectively we can turn that intelligence into benefits that people can actually experience.

r001.rationale: The response says people and organizations need time to adapt, but it does not mention the steam engine or that society may have taken decades or centuries to absorb its changes.
